Section on the Emergence from the Earth, analyzed through three gates:
first, the purpose of its inclusion; second, the explanation of the title; third, the resolution of difficulties. Regarding the purpose of its inclusion: [The text continues...]
Third:

First, within the section on the circulation of the study and practice of the seven chapters, the first chapter elucidates the practices to be studied, while the subsequent six chapters elucidate the persons who can practice them.

The practitioners among humanity can be divided into four categories; this present chapter specifically clarifies those who possess the practice of peaceful conduct (*sukhavihāra*) and propagate [the teaching].
The "Life Span" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa*) and "Distinguishing Merits" (*Guṇaparikīrtana*) chapters arise sequentially to resolve these doubts.

The "Rejoicing" (*Anumodanā*) and "Merits of the Dharma Master" (*Dharmabhāṇakaguṇa*) chapters clarify the merits obtained by those who assist and rely upon the person propagating the practice of peaceful conduct.

The "Chapter on Never-Disparaging" explains how the Buddha himself, while formerly dwelling in the stage of a causal practitioner, practiced the "Peaceful Conduct," cultivated patience, and so forth to propagate this sutra; having now attained the fruit of Buddhahood, he exhorts all sentient beings to diligently practice and study accordingly, and thus this chapter follows.

Second, within the two chapters that clarify the practice of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), the preceding chapter clarifies the practice to be performed, while this chapter clarifies the person who performs it; therefore, this chapter follows.

Third, the Treatise states: "Seventh, because of the manifestation of the unsurpassed teaching and transformation of sentient beings, immeasurable Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas emerge from within the earth."

In this section, it is clarified that the Buddha has already taught immeasurable bodhisattvas to practice these four practices; they have emerged from the earth to uphold this sutra and exhort all sentient beings, asking why they do not study them. For this reason, this chapter follows.

Regarding the explanation of the title: "Surging" (*yǒng*) means ascending upward; "Emergence" (*chū*) means manifesting. Because they ascend from the earth and manifest, it is titled the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth."
The *Yupian* states: "Yǒng means to surge upward.
Since surging is like water rising upward, it should be written as "yǒng" (湧).
"Yǒng" (踴) means to leap with bare feet; it does not carry the meaning of surging upward.
Regarding the resolution of this objection: Why is it not said that [the Bodhisattvas] come from the side, but rather that they leap forth from the earth?
Answer:
It clarifies that by relying on the four practices (*catur-yoga*), they uphold the sutra and thus leap forth from the ground of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Furthermore, it clarifies that they did not depart from this realm, as they had already transcended the ground of birth and death and were beings previously transformed by the Buddha;
thus, it does not say they came from the side, but only says they leaped forth from the earth.
The Sūtra states: "At that time, those from other directions arrived," and so forth, up to the detailed exposition.
The commentary says:
Within this chapter, the main text is divided into four sections.
First, the invitation from another land; second, the Tathāgata’s refusal; third, the emergence from this realm; fourth, the arising of doubt in the bodhisattvas.
This is the first [section]. The Sūtra states:
"At that time, the Buddha addressed [the assembly]... [up to] the extensive exposition of this sūtra."
The commentary states:
The Tathāgata did not permit this.
There are two [reasons]:
The first part establishes the prohibition, while the latter clarifies its intent.
This is stated as the maximum limit for the sake of brevity; thus it says "sixty thousand," though in reality it is not merely that many.
Clarifying the Buddha’s transformative merit serves to stop others from permitting [the act]; even if one causes others to protect [the precept], what fault could there be?
Regarding the sūtra passage, "At that time, when the Buddha had spoken thus, they simultaneously leaped forth," the commentary states:
There are eight ways in which beings emerge from this direction.

1. One leaped forth from the earth; 2. another ascended into the air to offer praise and prostration; 3. through supernatural power, time was shortened; 4. all the people beheld them together; 5. the Guide questioned them; 6. the World-Honored One comforted and answered them; 7. the four men expressed their sympathetic joy; 8. the Tathāgata praised them.
The initial section is divided into five parts:
first, the splitting of the earth; second, the leaping of the sages; third, the marks and signs of excellence; fourth, the dwelling place; and fifth, the assembly.
This [passage] concerns the first two.
The earth split open because they manifest the destruction of birth and death; they surged upward because they manifest the progression toward Bodhi.
Regarding the Sūtra’s statement, "These bodhisattvas reached the void and remained there," the commentary says:
These marks and embellishments, as well as the dwelling place, are the fruits obtained through practicing the practice of peace and bliss.
The marks and embellishments realize true nature, and by attaining the One Vehicle, one dwells in emptiness.
Regarding the sūtra passage, "These bodhisattvas reach that which cannot be known," the commentary says:
This refers to this multitude.
There are three parts:
first, the introduction; second, the enumeration of the categories; third, the conclusion.
The enumeration consists of eight classes:
One *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*, two parts of a *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*, three *nayuta*, four ten-thousands, five thousands, six hundreds, seven tens, and eight units.
The Sūtra states: "These bodhisattvas approached the two World-Honored Ones.
The commentary says:
This is the second instance of ascending into the air to offer praise and prostration.
There are three [acts]:
first, approaching the stupa; second, prostrating at its feet; and third, reverently praising it.
The sutra states: "These bodhisattvas arrive, which is to say, for about half a day."
The commentary states:
This is the third supernormal power.
There are three ways of shortening time:
First, the praise lasts for a long duration; second, the reception [of that praise] also lasts for a long time; third, it is a brief duration.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* explains that the kalpas, days and nights, months, seasons, and years mentioned in this sutra are calculated by combining day-and-night units. Thus, twenty-five days do not fail to constitute fifty minor kalpas (*antarakalpa*), or likewise fifty days, five months, and even full years. This is because when praising virtues, the deeper the merit, the longer the duration required for it to be fully known, and the supernatural power of receiving such praise is likewise equal [to the duration].

When praising [the Buddha], his supernatural power transformed their original perception of time; through his holy penetration, he extended or shortened the duration of light and shadow. Since sentient beings forget their fatigue when they love the Dharma, how much more so would they feel no weariness when the Sage secretly bestows his grace? Therefore, the fourfold assembly perceived it as lasting only the time of a meal.
Sustained by the nourishment of the Dharma and governed by supernormal powers, their life-span remains undiminished throughout many kalpas.
As the Sūtra says: "At that time, the fourfold assembly arrived at the void of the land."
The commentary states:
The fourth [category] is that which is commonly seen by all people.
The Sūtra says: "Among this assembly of bodhisattvas... up to... the teachers who lead and guide."
The commentary says:
Fifth, the inquiry of the Guide.
This section has four parts:
First, the enumeration of names; second, the virtuous conduct; third, the direct examination; and fourth, the inquiry by verse.
These are the first two [sections].
Because his conduct is lofty, supreme, and vast—being free from evil and advancing toward goodness—it is called the "fourfold."
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "In the presence of the great assembly" to "until weariness arises," the commentary states:
[This consists of] three sections on direct inquiry and four verses of questioning.
The *Yupian* states: "Xùn (訊) means to inquire, to address, and to speak. To interrogate by holding someone, or to communicate through inquiry, is called xùn.
The Sūtra says: "At that time, the World-Honored One... until he entered the Buddha-wisdom."
The commentary states:
The sixth World-Honored One provides a comforting response.
This consists of two parts:
First is the brief statement, followed by the explanation.
Within the explanation, there are three parts:
first, seeing the excellence of the Buddha’s tree; second, immediately receiving transformation through his teaching; third, meeting him indirectly and likewise following him.
Although they did not comply at first, they eventually complied later.
The first two [verses] praise the Bodhisattvas, while the last one speaks of the Śrāvakas.
Alternatively, the first two speak of indirect convergence, while the last one speaks of the inclination toward quiescence.
"Those who do not delude themselves regarding the Dharma" refers to entering into an understanding of the Buddha’s wisdom, not yet attaining its realization.

This is the first [section].

As the sutra says: "Even if each of these bodhisattvas were to arrive, they would still be unable to know them all exhaustively."
The commentary states:

One verse provides the general summary, seven verses provide the detailed exposition, and one verse provides the conclusion.

This is the practice of transformation.

This consists of an initial praise followed by a subsequent consent;
this is the former.
"Ajita" means "Unconquerable," which is the name of Maitreya.
“Ajita” is a corruption. The sutra says:
“You all should together go to the power of Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
The commentary states:
The following is permitted.
There are two [types], as indicated here in the prose:
"Donning the armor of diligence. Armor refers to military equipment such as coats of mail and helmets; it causes the mind to be courageous and keen, and to take joy in hearing the Dharma.
A mind that does not regress is called "firm resolve.
Because its meaning is profound and far-reaching, there is concern that one might become doubtful or retreat.
This explains the four powers:

First is the power of wisdom, which refers to the secret dharma and the two bodies of recompense of the Tathāgata as described in the "Chapter on the Lifespan," because they are the nature and marks of gnosis.
Second is the power of supernormal faculties, which refers to those very supernormal faculties and the emanation bodies of the Buddha.
The three powers of *vega* (swift exertion) refer to actions performed with certainty.
The character "奮" (*fen*) is pronounced *fu wen* (with the final nasalized);
it means to raise up or manifest. The character "迅" (*xun*) is pronounced *xi jin* (or *song run*); it means rapidity.
Now, returning from what follows:
when a lion intends to perform a definitive act, he first rouses himself, causing the hair on his body to stand erect, and swiftly arching his hindquarters before finally acting;
this clarifies that I now definitively declare the wondrous deeds of my own three bodies.
Fourth is the power of majesty (*pratāpa*): it correctly performs what is to be done, demonstrating all forms of majestic subjugation and destruction in order to crush those who lack faith.
Alternatively, it is "swift" (*vega*) by virtue of wisdom and "majestic" (*pratāpa*) by virtue of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Alternatively, for the wise, the two bodies—the Dharma-body and the Reward-body—and the three lower [bodies]—the Emanation-body—are the respective functions of the three wheels: miraculous transformations, knowledge of others' minds, and instruction.
Regarding the sūtra passage from "At that time, the World-Honored One [spoke]" up to "you all should listen with a single mind," the commentary states:
The first two verses exhort one not to harbor doubts and grant permission to speak; the latter two verses reveal the Buddha’s truthful words and admonish one to listen with a single mind.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "At that time, the World-Honored One" up to "causing them to resolve upon the Way," the commentary states:
This concludes the sixth section, the direct response.
There are three parts:
first, the announcement of my transformation; second, the clarification of the stages and dwellings; and finally, the concluding verse which exhorts the generation of faith.
This is the first part.
The Sūtra states: "These bodhisattvas... up to right mindfulness.
The Commentary says:
The following clarifies the dwelling and practice.
There are six [categories], which comprise two:
first, the place of abiding, and second, the interpretation of the sūtras.
"Thorough mastery" refers to the wisdom of hearing; "contemplation" refers to the wisdom of reflection; and "recollection" refers to the wisdom of cultivation.
Regarding the passage from the Sūtra, “Ajita, go and seek the unsurpassed wisdom,” the commentary states:
This consists of four parts.
First, delighting in tranquility; second, diligence; third, delighting in profound wisdom; fourth, seeking unsurpassed insight. As the sutra says:
"At that time, the World-Honored One... [omitted] ...caused them to resolve upon the mind of the Great Way."
The commentary states:
Seven and a half verses summarize the preceding section.
This is divided into five parts; this first half-verse indicates the Buddha’s transformation.
Regarding the Sūtra passage from "These are my sons" up to "for the sake of seeking the Buddha-way," the commentary states:
the first half-verse concerns delighting in tranquility, while the latter verse concerns diligence.
The character "kuì" (憒) has the phonetic reading *gǔ duì* (古對反); it means mental confusion.
The character "nào" (鬧) has the phonetic reading *nú xiào* (奴効反).
To be unsettled is "nào," which is also written with the character "nào."
Regarding the passage from "In the Sahā world" to "all shall eventually attain Buddhahood," the commentary states:
The first one and a half verses concern the dwelling place and profound wisdom; the final two verses conclude with the formation of my transformation.
Regarding this site of Gayā, those who were transformed here in the past are not the same as those currently at Gayā.
It is like saying one always dwells on Vulture Peak; it is not that the mountain always dwells there, but rather because [the Buddha] dwells upon the mountain.
This city is also like that.
Regarding the passage from the Sūtra, “I now speak words of truth... up to ‘to transform such multitudes as these’,” the commentary says:
A concluding exhortation to give rise to faith.
The Sūtra says: "At that time, Maitreya [attained] up to *samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The commentary states:
The seventh section on the mindfulness of the assembly.
The sutra states: “He addressed the Buddha, saying... until more than forty years had passed.
The commentary says:
The eighth petition has two parts;
the first is the long prose section, which has three sub-sections:
First, the objection is raised by citing the facts; next, it is raised by citing an analogy; finally, the objection is formally presented.
The first section has two parts:
first, citing the location and the year of his attainment of enlightenment; second, formally presenting the objection.
This is the first [section].
As for "the city of Gayā," it is extremely rugged and fortified, with few inhabitants; there are only slightly less than a thousand Brahmins, all of whom are descendants of the lineage of ṛṣis.
He does not serve kings or nobles, yet he is revered by both the high and the low; his city-dwelling is superior and powerful, known throughout the entire nation.
He resides within the borders of the kingdom of Magadha, very close to the south of the Buddha’s Bodhi tree; therefore, it is said that he is not far away.
Furthermore, it is said that Gayā is the birthplace of the Buddha and the capital city of the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
Since the Buddha attained enlightenment under the Bodhi tree in the kingdom of Magadha, and both locations are within Central India and extremely close to one another, it is said to be "not far."
Regarding the statement, "Since attaining great enlightenment until now, more than forty years have passed," there are briefly two explanations for this meaning:
first, there is the teaching of certain schools that he left home at nineteen and attained the Way at thirty.
The *Benqi yinguo jing* states that he left home at nineteen;
the *Sīwúxiāng sānmèi jīng* states that he attained enlightenment at thirty;

and the *Dazhidu lun* states: "When the Buddha was on the verge of entering nirvana, he told Subhadra: 'I left home at nineteen to seek the path of the Buddha; since leaving home, fifty years have passed.'"
The time of his attaining enlightenment was not specified.
In reality, the Buddha was eighty years old.

There is an interpretation which states: he left home at nineteen; thereafter, for five years he attended upon sages and practiced the "joyful conduct" (*sukhallikānuyoga*); for six years he practiced asceticism; thus, he attained enlightenment at thirty, and so told Subhadra that he had passed fifty years [since his renunciation].
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* employs this meaning and explains it accordingly.
When it is said here that he attained enlightenment forty years ago, he was only seventy years of age.
Secondly, various schools as well as Mahāyāna texts state that he left home at twenty-nine and attained enlightenment at thirty-five.

The *Ekottarika Āgama*, the *Madhyama Āgama*, the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, the *Udānavarga*, and the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* all state that he left home at twenty-nine; the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* and the *Samantapāsādikā* both state that he attained enlightenment at thirty-five.
The *Benqi jing* (Sutra on the Original Events) states:
"When the Buddha was about to renounce the world, he pointed to Yaśodharā’s belly and said:
'Six years from now, you shall give birth to a son.'"
"Thus he conceived Rāhu.
It was on the night the Buddha attained enlightenment after six years of ascetic practice that Rāhu was born.

Since it is only said that Rāhu remained in the womb for six years and not that he stayed in his mother’s belly for eleven years, we know that he left home at twenty-nine and attained enlightenment at thirty-five; during those six years, he practiced both the path of pleasure and the path of exertion: at the hermitage of Ārāḍa Kālāma, he attained the concentration of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*), and at the hermitage of Udraka Rāmaputra, he studied and attained the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samādhi*).
The Dharma Master Bodhiruci cited a verse from a sutra, saying:

"Eight years as an infant, Seven years as a youth, Four years studying the five sciences, Ten years indulging in the five desires, Six years practicing austerities, Thirty-five years to attain enlightenment, And forty-five years thereafter, He taught and transformed all sentient beings."

The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha, as well as his preceptor, the *Record of the Western Regions*, and other sources, all state that he left home at twenty-nine and attained enlightenment at thirty-five.
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states that the Buddha’s lifespan was eighty years.
The statement that he attained enlightenment more than forty years ago means that he was then seventy-five years old;
adding this to his initial year of attaining enlightenment, it totals forty-one years, which is what is meant by "more than forty."
Regarding the sūtra passage, "World-Honored One, how [does one attain] up to perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi)," the commentary states:
Below, the objection is formally set forth.
There are two parts:
first, the presentation of the three matters; second, the conclusion regarding the difficulty of belief.
Regarding the presentation of the three matters:
First, the matter is great; second, the time is brief and the multitude is vast; third, the duration is short yet virtue prevails.
This refers to the first point.
Having already attained the higher stage and being destined to realize *bodhi*, it is called "the matter is great."
The Sūtra says: "The World-Honored One arrived, yet could not find its limit.
The commentary states:
This refers to the brevity of time and the great number [of beings].
Preface: The phrase "in this short time" runs through the following two passages.
The Sūtra states: "These [beings], after a long period... until they constantly practice the holy life.
The Commentary says:
The duration is short, yet the virtue is supreme.
Observe that, having encountered conditions over a long period, they have planted roots of goodness; this was not cultivated for a brief time.
As the Sūtra says: "World-Honored One, this is difficult for the world to believe."
The commentary states:
This forms a point difficult to believe.
Due to these three matters, the Buddha’s transformation is difficult to believe.
The Sūtra says, "For example, there is a person for whom this matter is difficult to believe.
The Commentary states:
This is the second section, citing an analogy to raise an objection.

"Beautiful complexion" is a metaphor for the Buddha’s physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa* and *anuvyañjana*) being adorned; "black hair" signifies that even at the age of eighty, the Buddha lacks the signs of aging, for he remains excellent at all times as he traverses his former haunts.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, among the eighty minor marks, states:
"He is eternally youthful and does not age; he likes to visit old sites.
The phrase "twenty-five years of age" signifies that although the Buddha has transcended birth and death, he manifests as dwelling within the twenty-five realms of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
The above representation indicates that the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment was extremely recent;
even though he was eighty years old, he appeared like a twenty-five-year-old man, representing the high virtue and distant rank of the bodhisattvas he transforms, adorned with the hundred blessings.
"To say that I have given birth to him and caused his Way to grow is something difficult to believe.
The Sūtra says, "The Buddha is also like this... it is most rare indeed.
The commentary states:
The third section below formally presents the doubt.
It consists of three parts:

first, the restatement of the matter being doubted; second, from "Today" onwards, the formal presentation of the intent of the doubt; and third, from "Although we... onwards, the explanation of the reasons for the doubt.
This is the first [section], which has two parts:
first, restating that the time for the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment was brief; second, restating that the seven virtues of the Bodhisattva were exceedingly great.
The seven virtues of a bodhisattva are:

first, a long duration of practice; second, diligent vigor; third, mastery over meditative concentration; fourth, the attainment of supernormal powers; fifth, having long cultivated the holy life; sixth, the ability to study the Dharma; and seventh, skill in questioning and answering;
therefore, they are a treasure for humanity.
Regarding the sutra passage, "Today the World-Honored One has arrived for a matter of great merit," the commentary states:
This precisely articulates the intent of the doubt.
The Sūtra says: "Even though we have come here, we do not give rise to doubt.
The Commentary states:
This explains the reason for the arising of doubt.
There are three parts:
first, clarifying one's own capacity for penetration; second, presenting the arising of others' delusions; and third, formally requesting the removal of doubts and resolutions.
Although he himself has no doubts, because the manifested signs are not yet fully understood, he requests a resolution to his own uncertainty.
One has faith in the teachings spoken according to what is appropriate, because they are accomplished through faith.
One penetrates that which the Buddha knows, because it is accomplished through realization.
The Buddha’s words are not in vain, because they are free from the four errors.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from “At that time Maitreya” up to “expounded with accurate discrimination,” the commentary states:
The following fourteen verses are divided into three parts.

The first five verses present the objection by citing actual instances; the next two verses present the objection by means of a simile; and the final seven verses present the request for clarification following the expression of doubt.
This is the first [section], which has three parts:

One verse concerns the proximity of the time for renunciation; three verses concern the high station of the Bodhisattva’s virtues and the difficulty of believing them; one verse concerns the great assembly requesting a definitive resolution.
As the Sūtra says: "For example, it is like a young man whom the whole world does not believe."
The commentary says:
This verse is a metaphor.
The phrase "hair turning white and face wrinkling" serves to mutually illuminate and clarify the preceding prose.
The father spoke of his fine complexion and black hair, citing these as signs of his former virtuous conduct;
the son described his white hair and wrinkled face, characterizing them as marks of long cultivation yet still incomplete.
This was because the white hair bore witness to his long practice of the Noble Path, while the wrinkles indicated that his *lakṣaṇas* (physical marks of excellence) were not yet fully perfected.
The character "zhòu" (wrinkle) is pronounced with the initial *cè* and the final *jiù*.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra: "The World-Honored One likewise proceeded in this manner until he reached the lower void and stayed there," the commentary says:
The following seven verses present a request based on doubt.
This section is divided into two parts:
the first four verses set forth the matters regarding which there is doubt, and the final three verses formally present the request born of that doubt.
This is the first [section], which has three parts:
the first half-verse concerns the Buddha’s proximity to enlightenment; the next three verses praise the Bodhisattva for possessing ten virtues; and the final half-verse clarifies the dwelling place.
Regarding the sūtra passage, "We have heard from the Buddha... up to abiding in the stage of non-retrogression," the commentary states:
This correctly sets forth the request arising from doubt.
It consists of four parts:

the first half-verse shows that one has no doubts oneself; the next half-verse shows that others have delusions; the next verse shows the loss incurred by those who doubt; and the final verse is the formal request.
The Chapter on Life Span is analyzed through three gates:
first, the purpose; second, the explanation of the title; and third, the resolution of difficulties.
There are five points regarding the purpose:

First, within the circulation of the seven chapters on study and practice, the latter six chapters concerning those who can practice are divided into four parts; the second section, comprising the "Life Span" and "Distinguishing Merits" chapters, arises sequentially as an explanation to resolve preceding doubts.
Previously, when it was explained that those who leaped forth were all transformations of the Buddha, the assembly—being of high status and great number—naturally gave rise to doubt.

Now, having distinguished that the Dharma-body is fundamentally without arising or ceasing, while the transformation-buddhas are recently manifested and the reward-body has long been realized, what cause for doubt could there be regarding these transformations within this assembly?
Therefore, following the "Emergence" chapter, the "Life Span" chapter is elucidated.
Second, among the nineteen chapters that constitute the main body of the teaching, the final five chapters clarify the fruit of the One Vehicle.
The middle section is divided into two parts:
the first two chapters clarify the fruition already perfected, while the latter three chapters clarify the fruition not yet perfected.
Within the former of these, there are again two sub-sections.
The first part clearly elucidates the fruit already perfected; the latter part distinguishes how the assembly at that time attained various realizations based on this.
Therefore, this chapter follows.

Thirdly, the treatise states that among the seven types of pride to be countered, the seventh—where a person devoid of merit does not accumulate roots of goodness in the First Vehicle and yet does not acknowledge it as such—is the first form of *adhimāna* (conceit).
To counteract this, the analogy of the physician is taught.
The treatise further states that the seventh person is one whose faculties are not yet matured; for the sake of maturing them, the measure of nirvāṇa is manifested.

Those who have not yet accumulated roots of goodness are said to have "immature faculties. To cause them to accumulate various roots of goodness and aspire to the Supreme Vehicle, the Buddha manifests the limits and measures of his entry into nirvana, so that they may first accumulate roots of goodness and only thereafter be tamed and transformed.
Since the physician is treated in this chapter, this chapter follows.
Fourth, the treatise states that the eighth [chapter] demonstrates the attainment of supreme great enlightenment, thereby demonstrating the three types of Buddha-enlightenment.
The three bodies are present herein; therefore, this chapter follows.
This constitutes a fragment of the text, for among the seven similes, only the latter portion concerning the physician is explained, while the initial portion concerning the three Buddhas is not.
Fifth, because the ninth [chapter] manifests the unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*, the analogy of the physician is taught.

Regarding the mention of the physician among the seven types of pride: it refers to manifesting entry into extinction (*parinirvāṇa*) to ripen the faculties of those whose faculties are not yet mature.

Now, it is said that the physician—the Buddha—manifests entry into *nirvāṇa*; this is a manifestation of extinction while in reality there is no extinction. It is not like the extinction of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), which is a true extinction; therefore, it is called "unsurpassed. This is the remaining meaning among the seven analogies.
Regarding the explanation of the names: "Tathāgata" is the general name for the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body.
"Life-span" (āyuṣ) refers to the life one has received.
"Measure" (pramāṇa) signifies a fixed limit.

This chapter elucidates the limits of the life-span and essence of the three bodies of the Buddha, which—relying on the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), following the conditions of vows, responding to the capacities of sentient beings, and assuming their respective forms—are now clarified as the limits of the life-span of these three Buddhas;
therefore, it is titled the "Chapter on the Life-Span of the Tathāgata."
The character "shòu" (壽) is pronounced with the initial *zhì* and final *-you*.

The character "liàng" (量) is pronounced with the initial *lǚ* and final *-zhāng*; it refers to evaluating and comparing the lifespan of the Buddha—namely, praising or disparaging, calculating and deliberating upon the life spans of the three Buddhas.
Alternatively, "liàng" (讓) may be read as "fǎn" (反); the meaning is as explained previously, hence it is titled the "Chapter on Life Span.
To resolve an objection: why is the physician not used as the chapter title, but rather "life span" is adopted as the designation?
Answer:

It is because the lifespan of the three bodies serves as the cause that the physician is used as a metaphor; therefore, the name is derived from the fundamental measure of lifespan, rather than using "physician" as the title of the chapter.

Furthermore, there is an objection: the first section of the chapter states that the Buddha’s lifespan was first set forth in order to eliminate the overweening pride of those whose faculties were not yet mature and who had not accumulated merit.
Why, then, is this not the primary teaching (zhengzong) of the *Lotus Sūtra*, but rather subsumed under the section on propagation (liutongfen)?
Answer:
Because it was suited to the occasion and timely, it brought the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) to immediate maturity; as it was precisely tailored for the Śrāvakas, it constitutes the primary teaching.
However, because it was taught after the Teacher’s parinirvāṇa to those whose initial faculties were not yet mature, it is not the primary exposition.
Therefore, although he spoke of the lifespan, he did not bestow a prediction of enlightenment upon the śrāvakas;
likewise, although he spoke of the physician, there was no prediction for the śrāvakas either.
This is because the wise Mañjuśrī had previously requested to return; otherwise, why would he have requested to return midway so quickly?
Therefore, this chapter is merely for the purpose of dissemination; there is no contradiction in designating it as the main body of the teaching.
The Sūtra states: "At that time, the Buddha spoke these words of utmost sincerity and truth."
The commentary states:
This chapter has three parts:
first, Śākyamuni’s three exhortations; second, Maitreya’s four requests; and third, the Tathāgata’s formal instruction.
This is the first [point].
The wondrous essence of the three bodies reaches its ultimate state in the fruit; even those of superior wisdom cannot fathom it, so how could those of inferior ignorance understand it?
Fearing that their minds might harbor doubts and their mouths utter slanders, thereby causing injury to the Dharma, I have issued these earnest instructions before presenting this correct exposition.
Furthermore, there was concern that their ears might not be focused on the Dharma teachings and their minds might not be directed toward the profound mystery (xuanzong).

Moreover, because the natures of sentient beings are dull and they cannot understand upon merely hearing it, the Buddha repeatedly instructed and explained the three bodies (trikāya) so that the Dharma would enter their hearts; thus, he gave the threefold proclamation.
The Sūtra states: "At that time, the Bodhisattva, with profound faith, accepted the Buddha’s words.
The Commentary says:
These are Maitreya’s four requests.

Since the Buddha had already compassionately made three proclamations, how could the great assembly remain silent? Therefore, they added four requests to manifest the gravity of their aspiration for the Dharma.

The three proclamations indicate the teaching of the three bodies (*trikāya*); the four requests for each of the three bodies signify praying for the four virtues, aspiring for the four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*), and rescuing the four types of beings—this is the intended meaning.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "At that time the World-Honored One" up to "by the power of his supernormal faculties," the commentary states:
Below this is the Tathāgata’s direct instruction.
The initial prose section is divided into two parts:
first, the command to listen and the presentation of the topic; second, the actual exposition of the lifespan.
This is the former.
"Three requests" refers to the beginning [of the teaching].
"Secret" means that the two bodies—the Dharma-body and the Reward-body—are profound and subtle in essence.
"Supernatural powers" (ṛddhi) means that the Transformation-body manifests in response to sentient beings.

That which is concealed and protected by the Buddha is called "secret" (mi); that whose meaning is profound and difficult to understand is called "esoteric" (mi); its wondrous functioning without fixed method is called "divine" (shen); and its essence being free from obstruction is called "penetrating" (tong).
These two essences possess a majestic power that is difficult to subdue; therefore, they are termed "powers" (li).
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma* and other treatises state that there are four types of secrets; all of these secrets of the Buddha within the Vaipulya [sūtras] should be definitively resolved:

first, the secret of causing entry, which means teaching that form and so forth exist for the sake of śrāvakas so that they may enter the holy teaching gradually without fear, yet it does not mean that everything exists.

The second is the secret of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-guhya*), which means that based on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), it is taught that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), unarisen, and non-ceasing; this refutes the grasped existence of characteristics by describing them as non-existent, yet it does not mean that everything is non-existent.

Third, regarding the removal of misconceptions through the secret [teachings]: for the sake of removing various faults, the Buddha has taught diverse doctrines; specifically, he taught the Supreme Vehicle (Mahāyāna) to remove eight obstacles:
first, to remove the disparagement of the Buddha;
second, to remove the disparagement of the Dharma, by teaching that "I was formerly named the Tathāgata Vipaśyin," because there is no difference between [that name] and the Dharmakāya.
Third, to eliminate indolence, as it is said that those who vow to be born in the world of Ultimate Bliss shall all attain rebirth there;
fourth, to eliminate complacency with minor virtues by either praising or disparaging a single root of goodness;
fifth, to eliminate greedy conduct by extolling the richness, bliss, and adornment of the Buddha-fields.
Sixth, to eliminate the obstacle of prideful conduct, he praises the Buddhas or speaks of their superior excellence;

seventh, to eliminate the obstacle of remorse that hinders the cultivation of virtue, he explains that although some sentient beings may commit acts of slighting or disparagement toward the Buddhas and others, they will nonetheless be reborn in the heavenly realms;

eighth, to eliminate the obstacle of indeterminate disposition, he causes them to abandon the inferior aspirations of the śrāvakas by prophesying that great śrāvakas shall attain Buddhahood, and further declares that there is but the One Vehicle and no second.

The fourth is the secret of transformation (*pariṇāmanā-guhya*): as it is said, one awakens by taking the non-solid to be solid; while well-established in perversion and afflicted by extreme defilements, one attains supreme enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*).
Such cryptic terminology as these should be understood in a different sense.

Herein, "secret" refers to the third pair, the "Secret of Elimination. This is because those who disparage the Buddha’s virtues, or those who act out of greed and pride, claim the bodies of other Buddhas as their own essence; it is for the sake of praising the Buddha that this is taught.
As the sutra says, "In the interval between these [Buddhas], the Buddha Dīpaṃkara was taught," and so forth—all such statements are made through skillful means (*upāya*) and analytical distinction.

Regarding what is called "supernormal power" (*abhijñā*): when there are many beings to be converted, he employs his spiritual power (*ṛddhi-bala*) to transform them and cause them to generate the aspiration for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).
Regarding the sūtra passage from "All the world [attains] up to perfect enlightenment" (sarvaloka-yāvat-samyaksambodhi),
the commentary states:
Below, the lifespan is correctly explained.
According to the treatise, this is divided into two sections:
first, clarifying that enlightenment (*bodhi*) is unsurpassed;

second, [the passage beginning with] "O sons of good family, as for the lifespan accomplished by me when I originally practiced the bodhisattva path," which further elucidates the distinct characteristics of the two bodies—the retributive and the transformational—as well as the unsurpassed nature of *nirvāṇa*.
Within the initial text, the treatise is divided into three sections to manifest the bodhi of the three Buddhas.
First is the *nirmāṇa-bodhi* (transformation bodhi), because it manifests according to what should be seen by those to be converted.
As the sutras all state, the Tathāgata departed from the palace of the Śākyas and, not far from the city of Gayā, sat at the site of enlightenment and attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Therefore, this very passage refers to it.
Second is the *saṃbhoga-buddha*’s bodhi: by fulfilling the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one attains eternal *nirvāṇa*.
As the sutra says: "Good son, since I truly attained Buddhahood, immeasurable, boundless, hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas have passed."
The following passage explains this third point:
the Bodhi of the Dharma-Buddha refers to the Tathāgatagarbha, which is the intrinsically pure Nirvāṇa, because it is eternal, constant, pure, and unchanging.

As the Sūtra states: "The Tathāgata knows and perceives the characteristics of the triple world as they truly are, yet he does not perceive the triple world as the triple world is perceived [by ordinary beings]."
"Why is this so? refers to the following passage.
This is based on the first "unsurpassed" [nature], which possesses the three bodies as its three meanings.

Regarding the increase or decrease of the Buddha-bodies, various teachings differ: sometimes they are collectively designated as the single Jewel of the Buddha, and sometimes they are distinguished into two.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"First, the birth-body; second, the dharma-body.
Both the dharma-body and the true recompense body are termed the "dharma-body," because they consist of actual merits.
The *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) are both termed the "birth-body" (*janmakāya*).
Furthermore, the *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* speaks of two types:
first, the true Buddha; second, that which is not the true Buddha.
The first is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); the latter two bodies may be further divided into three, which correspond to the three types of Buddha-enlightenment (*buddhabodhi*) explained here.
Alternatively, four types are taught; the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
first, the transformation-response Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*); second, the merit Buddha (*guṇa-buddha*); third, the wisdom Buddha (*jñāna-buddha*); and fourth, the suchness Buddha (*tathatā-buddha*).
The first is the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body), the middle two are the saṃbhogakāya (reward body), and the last one is the dharmakāya (dharma body).
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* further speaks of four types:

first, the "emanation that is not the response" (*nirmāṇa-asambhogika*). This refers to forms such as those of dragons or spirits manifested by the Buddha for the sake of sentient beings; because these are not the [actual] Buddha-body, they are called "emanations that are not responses."

Second, the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is not an emanation (*nirmita*). This refers to the Buddha-body perceived by bodhisattvas prior to the stages of the grounds (*bhūmi*), which manifests based on meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and is not subsumed within the five destinies (*pañcagati*); thus it is called a "response that is not an emanation. This is precisely the single response body within a great trichiliocosm perceived by those possessing the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*).
The third type is both a *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and a *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment body). This refers to the Buddha-body perceived by the various śrāvakas;
it is called a *nirmāṇakāya* because it is seen as being manifested through cultivation, and it is called an emanation because it appears as a being of the same class as humans.

The fourth is neither *nirmāṇa* (emanation) nor *pariṇāma* (transformation); this refers to the Buddha’s true body (*dharmakāya*). The first three are emanations, while the latter consists of the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* also speaks of four types:
first, the enjoyment body that is not a transformation, which refers to the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*).
Second, that which is transformational but not enjoyment, referring to the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) that manifests for those below the ten stages;
third, that which is both enjoyment and transformational, referring to the enjoyment body (saṃbhogakāya) that manifests for bodhisattvas of the ten stages;
fourth, that which is neither enjoyment nor transformational, referring to the dharma body (dharmakāya).
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speaks of ten types of Buddhas:
first is the Unattached Buddha (*asaṅga-buddha*), so called because he dwells peacefully in the world and attains perfect enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*).
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* names this the Manifestly Perfectly Enlightened Buddha (*abhisambuddha-buddha*).
The second is the Buddha of Vows, so called because he brings them forth.

He is named the Buddha of Great Aspirations; and the Buddha of the Retribution of the Three Karmas, so called because his faith is perfected—though all practices have causes, here only faith is mentioned.
He is named the Buddha of the Maturation of Karma.
Fourth is the Buddha of Sustenance (*dhāraṇī-buddha*), because he accords with the world without interruption;
he is called the Buddha of Abiding Sustenance (*sthiti-dhāraṇī-buddha*).
Fifth is the Buddha of Nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇa-buddha*), because he manifests parinirvāṇa.
The former is called the Transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*).
The sixth is the Dharma-realm Buddha (*dharmadhātu-buddha*), because there is no place where he does not manifest.
The seventh is the Mind Buddha (*citta-buddha*), because of his excellent abiding.
The two names above are the same as those [of the previous Buddhas].
The Buddha of the Eight Samādhis is so called because he has accomplished immeasurable merits and is free from attachment;
his name there is the Buddha of Concentration (Dhyāna).
Ninth is the Buddha of Nature, because of his excellent determination;
he is called the Buddha of Original Nature.
Tenth is the Buddha of Sovereign Will, because of his universal coverage.
That one is named the Buddha Anuruddha.
The first five are conventional Buddhas, while the latter five are ultimate Buddhas.
They are subsumed within the three bodies (trikāya) as appropriate: the first five are subsumed within the nirmāṇakāya, because they are designated as conventional.

The single category of the *dharmadhātu* is subsumed under the *dharmakāya*; the single category of "original nature" (*prakṛti*) pertains to both the *dharmakāya* and the *saṃbhogakāya*; and the remaining three categories pertain exclusively to the *saṃbhogakāya*.

The treatise states that these five are the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Although the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* differ in form from the aforementioned *nirmāṇakāya*, they are all nonetheless the ultimate truth.
Examine the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, specifically the "Chapter on Contemplating the Tathāgata," along with its commentaries.
The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* states:
"O Mahāmati!"

The Dharma-Buddha teaches the Dharma by being free from objective referents (*ālambana*), free from the duality of the observer and the observed, and free from the characteristics of conditioned activity and measurement. Mahāmati!

The Reward-Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) teaches that all phenomena possess both specific and general characteristics; because they arise from the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) manifested by one's own mind, he also says it is like a magician who conjures various forms and images through illusion.
Foolish people grasp at these as being real, yet those images are truly unobtainable; this is called the conceptualization of the unreal nature of phenomena.
Mahāmati!

The transformation Buddha (nirmāṇakāya-buddha) preaches the teachings of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as the factors of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
The *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"The transformation body is not the true Buddha, nor is it the speaker of the Dharma," and so forth; this is because all merit is attributed to the fundamental source, which is exclusively the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). Therefore, the central tenet of that sutra is the teaching of the true Dharma-body.

Taking advantage of the flow of the text, I have briefly clarified the meaning of "Buddha"; the realization of Buddhahood through the three bodies is as explained in the *Maitreya Commentary*, while the specific details are as set forth in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and the *Fayuan*.
Although it is said that the Buddha’s body varies in its increase or decrease, when categorized by type, there are no more than two kinds:
first, the true body (*dharmakāya*), and second, the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
That which is seen by bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and by those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) is called the transformation body.
The two bodies—the retributive body (*vipākakāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*)—are called the true body (*satyakāya*).
Based on this principle, within the enlightenment of the three Buddhas, a distinction is made between two parts:
first, clarifying the body perceived by those of the three vehicles and the doubts they harbor regarding it; second, clarifying the true body that those of the three vehicles do not know.
This is the first [section].
Regarding the sutra passage from "However, son of good family" up to "for *nayuta* kalpas," the commentary says:
The following clarifies the true body (dharmakāya), which is unknown to those of the three vehicles.
This section is divided into three parts;
first, it indicates the long duration since his attainment of enlightenment.
Next is the explanation of the period of time since attaining enlightenment;
following this is the conclusion of what was previously stated, beginning with: "In this way, since I attained enlightenment, a very long time has passed. This is that section.
This is the first point.

The commentary explains that only the reward body (sambhogakāya) attains enlightenment; however, according to reality, the cultivation and fulfillment of realization by the reward body is called "attainment," and the cultivation, manifestation, and perfect realization of the dharma body (dharmakāya) is also called "attainment. What fault could there be in this?
Although this section indicates that the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) is established as enduring, the subsequent explanation also clarifies the meaning of the *dharmakāya* (dharma body).
As the Sūtra says: "For example, from five hundred [to]... until one knows their number."
The commentary says:
The following explains the duration of time since attaining enlightenment.
There are two parts:
At the beginning, it clearly explains that the Buddha’s *bodhi* is a fruition; having attained enlightenment long ago, he speaks of it as being recent for the sake of sentient beings.

From the passage "Later, O sons of good family, regarding the sutras expounded by the Tathāgata" onwards, it secretly reveals the *dharmakāya*; because one realizes this, it is understood that while the attainment of the Way is in truth ancient, its manifestations are expediently displayed in accordance with the needs of beings.
The former is the wisdom that realizes, and the latter is the principle realized.
Wisdom and the qualities resulting from its severance, as well as the locus of wisdom, are clarified in their respective order.
The first section consists of three parts:
First, the analogy is posed as a question; next, Maitreya and others provide the answer; finally, the Buddha gives a detailed explanation.
This is the first part. The Sūtra states:
"Maitreya Bodhisattva... to immeasurable and boundless."
The commentary says:
This is Maitreya and others’ response.
It consists of three parts:
First, a general statement on the immeasurable; second, clarifying that the followers of the two vehicles do not know it; third, concluding on its boundlessness.
Some say "Aviveci," but it should be read as "Abhibhūci," meaning the stage of non-retrogression.
The Sūtra says: "At that time, the Buddha told [them]... up to incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
The Commentary states:
Below, the Buddha provides a detailed explanation.
This is divided into two parts:

first, the announcement that the *saṃbhogakāya* has actually attained enlightenment for a very long time; second, from "O sons of good family, during this interval... onwards, the announcement regarding the *nirmāṇakāya* which addresses those doubts and difficulties.
The initial section has two parts:
first, clarifying the kalpas since his attainment of enlightenment; second, clarifying the places where he constantly dwells.
This is the first part.
There are two parts:
first, the initial statement and announcement; second, the explanation of the kalpas.
The Sūtra says: "From that time until now, leading and benefiting sentient beings."
The commentary states:
This clarifies the dwelling place of the *svasaṃbhogakāya*.

Although the *svasaṃbhogakāya* actually pervades the entire *dharmadhātu* and its specific characteristics are difficult to perceive, it is nonetheless explained according to the limited perspectives of those with inferior capacities. To manifest its essence, its function is cited to indicate a "distinct location," for wherever the arising of its function occurs, the body itself is present there.

Furthermore, just as the characteristics of the vast, pervasive, and unobstructed expanse of empty space are manifested, so too is the place where the true recompense and the dharma-body are both perfectly realized made manifest; therefore, the functions of the self-recompense body are separately revealed.

Furthermore, it is said that this refers to the *parabhogakāya* (body of enjoyment for others) of the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, which is established as enduring by citing what is known to others, rather than being its own retribution.
This is from the sutra passage: "O sons of good family... up to the skillful differentiation."
The commentary states:
The following section addresses the doubts and difficulties concerning the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).
There are three parts:

First is the general introduction and explanation, second is the detailed explanation, and finally, from "Good sons, the Tathāgata perceives all sentient beings... onwards is the concluding explanation.
This is the first part.
Other assemblies may have doubts, saying:

Since attaining enlightenment long ago, you have constantly been teaching and transforming beings here; as for those who attained enlightenment, entered nirvana, and preached the Dharma to deliver sentient beings during that interval—such as Dīpaṃkara, Vipaśyin, and others—who were they?
The present commentary states:

"In this interval, it is taught that [Buddhas such as] Dīpaṃkara attained enlightenment and entered parinirvāṇa; all such instances are explained through the skillful means of wisdom as being other Buddhas, yet there are no such Buddhas existing apart from my own body."
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "All good sons" to "the sharpness or dullness of their faculties," the commentary states:
The following section provides a specific explanation to resolve doubts.
There are two parts:
first, clarifying the reason; second, from "according to those to be saved" onwards, revealing the distinctions.
This is the first part.
When sentient beings resolve their minds to practice and aspire to see the Buddha, they are said to have come to my presence.

Observing the distinctions between the sharpness and dullness of their five faculties, I tell those of sharp faculties that the realization of the Way is distant, while for those of dull faculties, I manifest that the realization of the Way is near;
for the sake of the sharp, I speak of attaining perfect enlightenment, and for the sake of the dull, I manifest entry into nirvana.
To benefit those of sharp faculties, he manifests a great body; to benefit those of dull faculties, he manifests a small body.
To benefit those of sharp faculties, he expounds the profound Dharma; to benefit those of dull faculties, he expounds the shallow Dharma.
In each case, according to what is appropriate, he manifests these distinctions in response to their perceptions.
The Sūtra states: "According to those to be converted, up to the arousal of a joyful mind.
The commentary says:
This reveals the distinctions.

Because the faculties and dispositions of those who have come differ, the World-Honored One himself speaks of their names as being distinct; the number of years since his attainment of enlightenment varies—whether long or short—and the dimensions of his body differ. These are manifestations of the different modes of attaining enlightenment and entering parinirvāṇa, as well as the different skillful means of teaching the One Vehicle, Two Vehicles, Three Vehicles, and Four Vehicles, all intended to bring joy to the minds of those beings.

It is just like the clarity of the sky and the brilliance of a jade disk, vast and boundlessly luminous; though the water may swirl and the radiance may reach its limits, when the water is clear the moon’s reflection appears, and when the water is turbid the moon’s reflection sinks. The reflections appear differently depending on whether the vessel is whole or broken, and there remains a distinction between darkness and light.
This is the distinction between the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body).
This passage has two interpretations:

first, that while the actual attainment of the path by Śākyamuni was long ago, this is a new manifestation of his emanation; second, that it does not contradict the "intention of equality" among the four intentions, nor the "secret of counteracting" among the four secrets. [These teachings] remove the obstacle of disparaging the Buddha-dharma and refute the pride of those who claim others as themselves; they praise the Buddhas, perhaps with exaggeration. Otherwise, before the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, who would have received the prediction?
This too is a manifested transformation; what contradiction could there be?
The Sūtra says: "O sons of good family, up to making such a statement.
The commentary states:
This is the explanation of the verse.
Because his goodness was slight, his virtue was meager; because his transgressions were many, his defilement was heavy.
He approached perfect enlightenment as if using a small vessel, yet he attained the Way long ago when confronted with great faculties and reality.
Because he employs skillful means to transform sentient beings and cause them to enter the Path, appearing from time to time to inspire longing and veneration.
As the Sūtra says: "O sons of good family, all [that I have said] is true and not false."
The commentary states:

Next, the second [section] concerns the secret teaching on the Dharmakāya. Because one realizes this, the attainment of the Way is in truth ancient, yet it manifests provisional means in response to sentient beings.
There are three [aspects].
The initial heading indicates that these various teachings expounded in response to sentient beings are all non-false proclamations.
The subsequent explanation clarifies that these can be manifested because of the realization of the *dharmakāya*; however, according to the ultimate truth, such things do not fundamentally exist.
Below the section beginning with "By means of all sentient beings," the reason for manifesting provisional [teachings] in response to objects is explained.
This first part has three sections:
First, the indication; second, the manifestation; third, the conclusion that it is not in vain.
"To speak" means verbal expression;
"to show" means to manifest.
"Body" refers to the internal physical form.
"Deeds" refers to karmic actions.
To speak of one's own body means to state that one's own body was once that of King Sattva, King Śibi, and so forth.

To speak of the bodies of others refers to cases such as when it is said that Maitreya was formerly the Rishi Sarvajñāprabha, or that Amitābha Buddha manifested as the Bhikṣu Dharmākara, and so forth.

To show one's own body refers to manifesting as the body of Śākyamuni appearing in the world oneself, or as in the case of Queen Śrīmālā, who invited the Buddha from afar to appear in the sky, and so forth.
"Manifesting the bodies of others" refers to appearing as Vipaśyin Buddha manifesting in the world, opening the stupa to reveal the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, and so forth.
"Manifesting one's own deeds" refers to appearing as Śākyamuni performing such activities as subduing Māra, attaining enlightenment, preaching the Dharma, and manifesting supernatural powers.

"Manifesting other deeds" refers to manifesting such activities as the Great Universal Wisdom-Victor (Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū) displaying supernormal powers, shaking the earth, emitting light, and attaining enlightenment.
These deeds he manifests in order to deliver sentient beings are all real and not false.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "For what reason? up to "there is no error," the commentary states:
This is because of the realization of the Dharmakāya.

However, in ultimate truth, such things do not exist at all; for what reason could there be anything to be taught or shown? All [teachings] are non-false because they arise from seeing this ultimate truth as it truly is.
This consists of five propositions, and the phrase "seeing according to reality" (yathābhūta-darśana) runs through all five.
The first proposition reveals the *dharmakāya* by relying on the locus of delusion.

The treatise states: "Regarding the characteristics of the three realms, it is said that the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*) is itself the realm of nirvāṇa; for there is no nature possessing the characteristic of the *tathāgatagarbha* apart from the realm of sentient beings."
The statement in the "Expedient Means" chapter that "the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding" refers precisely to this.
The second phrase reveals the *dharmakāya* by means of its eternal purity.
The treatise states: "There is no birth-and-death, neither departing nor emerging," which means it is eternally constant, pure, and unchanging.
"Retreat" refers to sinking into delusion; "emergence" refers to liberation from fetters, or alternatively, to arising and ceasing.
This means that while the phenomena of birth and death involve retreating and emerging, true reality is devoid of such things;
therefore, it is eternally pure.
The third phrase reveals the *dharmakāya* by way of being neither identical to nor separate from [sentient beings].

The treatise states: "There is neither one remaining in the world nor one who has entered parinirvāṇa. This refers to the essence of the *tathāgatagarbha*-true-suchness (*tathatā*), which is neither identical to the realm of sentient beings nor separate from the realm of sentient beings. Because it does not remain in the world, it is not identical to the realm of sentient beings; because it does not enter parinirvāṇa, it is not separate from the realm of sentient beings.
The fourth phrase reveals the *dharmakāya* by way of departing from the four characteristics.
The treatise states: "Neither real nor unreal, neither suchness nor different" means that it is free from the four kinds of characteristics, for these four characteristics are impermanent.

"The characteristic of arising is substantially existent; the characteristic of cessation is empty; the characteristic of abiding is suchness; and the characteristic of change is difference. Since the Dharma-body lacks these, all four are non-existent.
The fifth phrase reveals the Dharma-body by relying on the Buddha’s internal realization, which is not attainable by ordinary beings.
The Treatise states: "Those who do not perceive the three realms as the three realms are the Tathāgatas, who are able to see and realize the *tathatā* dharma-body, whereas ordinary beings do not.
Therefore, the Sūtra says that the Tathāgata perceives clearly and without error."
The commentary explains that this refers exclusively to the fifth phrase, which at first glance appears to be a summary of all the preceding phrases.

This phrase states that the Tathāgata’s correct wisdom can see with clarity; unlike the delusive appearances of the triple world, he is able to realize and perceive the *dharmakāya*—the *tathatā* (suchness) that is the essential nature of the triple world. Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata’s clear vision is without error.
The Sūtra says: "Because of all sentient beings... until never for a moment ceasing.
The Commentary states:
The following explains the reason why [the Buddha] manifests provisional means in response to sentient beings.
"Various natures" refers to the *dhātu* (elements).
"Desire" refers to resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).
"Conduct" refers to mental formations (*cittasaṃskāra*).
"Recollection and conceptualization" refers to the practices leading to all destinations.
Due to these factors, the Buddha's activities are never neglected, and thus various teachings are demonstrated.

It was previously stated that the *saṃbhogakāya* truly attains enlightenment after a long duration; however, because the Buddha perceives with his Buddha-eye the sharpness or dullness of their faculties, he demonstrates different teachings accordingly.

This teaching states that the Dharma-body is truly devoid of all characteristics; yet, because it accords with the differences in the dispositions and desires of sentient beings, it is manifested in various ways.
The Sūtra says: "In this way, I have attained [the state] up to being eternally abiding and imperishable."
The commentary states:
This clarifies the third conclusion regarding the true body (*dharmakāya*), which is unknown to those of the three vehicles, thereby completing the preceding discourse.
[This is shown in] the Sūtra from "O sons of good family" up to "further doubling the aforementioned number."
The commentary states:

The preceding section clarifies that Bodhi is unsurpassed; the second major section below further elucidates the distinct characteristics of the two bodies—the Reward Body and the Transformation Body—as well as the unsurpassed nature of Nirvana.
The middle section is divided into two parts:

first, an explanation through doctrine regarding the permanence and the arising and ceasing of the two bodies; second, an explanation through analogy regarding the permanence and the arising and ceasing of the two bodies.
The first part is further divided into two.

The first part clarifies that the two bodies are eternally abiding and neither arise nor cease; the subsequent section, beginning with "Furthermore, son of good family, the dharmas of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas are all thus," explains and establishes that the aforementioned teaching is naturally so and not false.
The initial section further has two parts:

first, it clarifies that because the *saṃbhogakāya* accords with the realms of sentient beings and the power of its original vows, its lifespan is eternally abiding; second, it clarifies that because the *nirmāṇakāya* accords with the bodies and inclinations of sentient beings, it manifests arising and ceasing.
This is the first point.

When he was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, he made a vow that he would enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* only after all sentient beings had been delivered; because the realm of sentient beings has no end, his attainment of the fruit is now perfect and his vows and practices have not withered. Therefore, his lifespan is inexhaustible and further doubles the aforementioned number.
Regarding the sūtra passage, "However, it is not that [the Buddha] has truly arrived, but rather he teaches and transforms sentient beings," the commentary states:
The following clarifies that the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body) manifests arising and ceasing in accordance with the bodies and mental dispositions of sentient beings.
There are three parts:
first, the heading;
second, the explanation.
The third section begins with: "Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks by means of skillful means.
This is the first [point].

Now, this Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) does not undergo actual parinirvāṇa; rather, it is a false proclamation that it shall enter parinirvāṇa, which is merely a manifestation of transformative marks (*nirmāṇalakṣaṇa*) through skillful means to convert sentient beings.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from "For what reason? up to "within the net of false views," the commentary states:
This is the subsequent explanation.
There are two parts:
first, clarifying that their nature is evil; second, clarifying that they further produce evil.
This is the first part.

There are six fundamental evils: first, having little merit, one cannot encounter superior persons or superior dharmas; second, not planting roots of goodness, one lacks the cause for the fruit of birth; third, being impoverished, one lacks wealth and the Dharma, resulting in a narrow mind and inferior aspirations; fourth, being of low station, one holds oneself in contempt; fifth, being intoxicated by the afflictions of attachment to desire; and sixth, entering the net of discursive thought and false views, where one possesses a deceptive cleverness and engages in erroneous conduct and confused study.
The Sūtra says: "If one sees the Tathāgata, one should give rise to a heart of supreme reverence.
The commentary states:
This clarifies that [such a person] will further produce evil.
There are five:
first, arrogance, indulgence, and heedlessness;
second, harboring weariness and taking no pleasure in approaching or accepting [others].
Third, harboring indolence, being entangled by laziness such that one cannot examine oneself;
fourth, not conceiving the thought that [the Buddha] is difficult to encounter, and failing to give rise to a sense of rare opportunity upon seeing the Buddha;
fifth, not giving rise to a mind of reverence, and failing to initiate the practice of compliant deeds out of yearning and aspiration.

This is said because, due to their inherently evil nature, they give rise to three further evils upon seeing the Buddha; consequently, they fail to conceive the thought that he is difficult to encounter, nor do they develop a heart of reverence.
The Sūtra says: "Therefore, the Tathāgata comes and speaks of extinction.
The commentary states:
This completes the lower [section].
There are three parts:
first, the heading; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion.
This corresponds to the Sūtra passage from "Furthermore, good son" up to "all is real and not false."
The commentary states:
This explains that the aforementioned teaching is inherently unfailing.
The meaning of this statement is that the *saṃbhogakāya* is by its very nature (*dharmatā*) vowed to deliver all sentient beings without exception, remaining eternally present and never ceasing.
It is the natural law that the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya), in accordance with the likes and dislikes, joys and regrets of sentient beings, manifests birth and death.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states, the Tathāgata does not enter nirvāṇa.
The verse says:
"Even if a crow and an owl were to perch together upon the same tree like close brothers, only then would you attain eternal nirvana."
Even if snakes, rats, and wolves were to roam together in a single hole, loving one another like brothers, only then would there be eternal nirvāṇa.
Even if an icchantika were to manifest and attain the Buddha-way, eternally experiencing the supreme bliss and only then enter parinirvāṇa—
since the Tathāgata regards all beings as he does Rāhula, how could he abandon his compassion and enter parinirvāṇa forever?
This final verse should be applied to each of the preceding three analogies; however, fearing that the text would become overly prolix, it is stated here in its entirety as one.
Thus, the three matters that are perfected upon entering Great Nirvāṇa are not attained by those of the Two Vehicles.
He manifests through transformation and enters extinction; having thus entered extinction, he again manifests in other realms and is born here once more.
Since his body and wisdom are neither permanently non-existent, how could he be the same as those of the Two Vehicles who enter extinction?
For this reason, it is called the unsurpassed nirvāṇa.
Regarding the sūtra passage, “It is like a skilled physician who thoroughly treats all manner of illnesses,” the commentary says:
The second section below provides an analogy for the permanence and the arising-and-ceasing of the two bodies.
It consists of two parts:
first, an analogy explaining permanence and arising-and-ceasing; second, an analogy consisting of questions and answers to demonstrate that this is not false.

There are twelve similes: first, the simile of skillfully discerning the capacities and circumstances; second, the simile of arising through compassionate pity to transform others; third, the simile of the Way being hidden while observing capacities; fourth, the simile of delusions arising upon encountering conditions; fifth, the simile of accomplishing the Way to save sentient beings; sixth, the simile of all rejoicing upon seeing the Buddha; seventh, the simile of preaching the Dharma in response to capacities; eighth, the simile of the faculties ripening and the Way being perfected; ninth, the simile of those not yet ripened feeling weary of the Dharma; tenth, the simile of causing them to long for the Buddha by manifesting his parinirvāṇa; eleventh, the simile of longing for the Buddha and loving the Dharma; twelfth, the simile of attaining the noble state and seeing the Buddha.
This is the first point.

Regarding the refinement of faculties (indriya-pariśodhana) among those of the Two Vehicles: those who attain few births are considered dull-witted, while those who attain many births are considered sharp-witted.
Regarding diligence and laxity: those who attain few births are considered sharp-witted, while those who attain many births are considered dull-witted.
Now the subsequent pairs are explained.
These first two similes correspond to those who, upon seeing the Buddha at birth, are taught together and give rise to the resolve for enlightenment.
The third and fourth similes correspond to those of the second capacity who, having ripened their roots and diligently practiced, do not lose their original resolve and cultivate gradually.
Those who are immature and indolent lose their original mind and regress.

The fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth analogies correspond to those of the third root-faculty who mature through diligent cultivation; they behold Śākyamuni Buddha and, having fulfilled the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), immediately give rise to the Great Mind and undergo the birth of transformation (*pariṇāmiki-jāti*).
Those who are immature and indolent, although they behold the present Buddha, have not yet realized [enlightenment] and remain in the rank of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

The tenth, eleventh, and twelfth [assemblies] together constitute the fourth birth for those whose faculties were previously immature and who were indolent; they shall all attain the Way upon encountering Maitreya Buddha, and having likewise resolved their great mind, they will first undergo the birth of transformation (*parivṛtti*).
Those whose faculties were mature and who attained the Way through diligence shall likewise behold that Buddha.
Therefore, it is said that both are enabled to see.
Maitreya is none other than myself, spoken of under a different name.
Alternatively, this may refer collectively to three lifetimes, with the first four similes illustrating this.
The "first birth" refers to when the Buddha first manifested his parinirvāṇa; those who did not see the Buddha then gave rise to afflictions (*kleśa*).

The subsequent five similes constitute the "second birth," which refers to the manifestation of parinirvāṇa within the time of Śākyamuni Buddha. Those whose faculties are mature and who diligently cultivate the path abide in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*); their gradual severing of afflictions is called "healing," yet it does not mean that all are completely severed so as to achieve the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
As for those whose faculties are not yet mature and who fall away, they still abide in the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and have not yet realized [the fruit].

The latter three parables represent the third birth; those with mature faculties who exert effort both attain the state of *aśaikṣa*, while those whose faculties are not yet mature and who fall away also attain the state of *śaikṣa*.

At the very end of these two cases, both saw Śākyamuni and simultaneously gave rise to the great resolve; therefore, within the predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), both *aśaikṣas* and *śaikṣas* are present together.
To manifest the existence of nirvana for such types of beings is the general purport of this analogy.
A skilled physician possesses four qualities:

first, knowing the nature of the disease; second, knowing the cause of the disease; third, knowing that once the disease has been extinguished, it will not arise again; and fourth, knowing that once the disease has been extinguished, it may arise again.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"Out of great compassion for sentient beings, I now take refuge in you; Because you skillfully extract the arrows of all poisons, You are called the Great King of Physicians."
The treatments administered by worldly physicians, though they may bring recovery, lead to illness arising once more; those treated by the Tathāgata shall never again fall ill.
The World-Honored One bestows the medicine of ambrosia upon all sentient beings; once they have taken it, they neither die nor are they born again.
Therefore, the Buddha is compared to a skilled physician. One with wisdom discerns and contemplates birth and death;

one who is sagacious responds to the capacities of beings to bestow salvation; one who is proficient in prescriptions and medicines is thoroughly conversant with the teachings and their principles; and one who skillfully treats all ailments such that they never recur—these correspond to the four virtues of a physician.
Regarding the sutra passage, "That person has many [beings], even numbering up to a hundred," the commentary states:
These two [passages] illustrate the arising of transformation through the arousal of compassion.
Only those possessing the seeds of the two vehicles are called "sons"; thus, the mention of ten or twenty includes those with the nature of bodhisattvas, as their status is indeterminate.
